title: Learning to Prompt in the Classroom to Understand AI Limits: A Pilot Study
extended_summary:
This paper examines how an AI literacy intervention can help adolescents better understand the capabilities and limitations of large language models such as ChatGPT, while also reducing fear and negative attitudes toward AI. The authors argue that public excitement about LLMs often coexists with misleading assumptions that these systems can reliably solve problems across domains, despite known weaknesses such as hallucinations, limited reasoning, and imperfect instruction-following. The study therefore asks whether a classroom-based prompting workshop can improve students’ interactions with ChatGPT and foster a more realistic understanding of AI.

The intervention was a two-hour school workshop combining instruction and hands-on practice. Students first received a presentation on intelligence, AI, and LLMs, then completed an activity using ChatGPT to act as a personal teacher explaining the concept of democracy in an engaging way. This initial activity was designed to expose limitations in ChatGPT’s ability to follow complex instructions. The instructor then explicitly discussed ChatGPT’s limits and introduced prompting strategies, after which students completed a second, similar prompting activity. Data collection included pre/post questionnaires on perceived AI threat, post-workshop self-reported emotions, user-experience ratings, perceptions of ChatGPT functionality, and open-ended responses about the interaction.

The study involved 21 high school students aged 16 to 18 in a formal school setting in Palermo, Sicily, Italy. The context was a single high school workshop rather than a full curricular implementation. The activity was teacher- or instructor-led, with guided practice using ChatGPT during class time. Although the paper is relevant to K-12 AI literacy and classroom uses of generative AI, it is not primarily a literacy-instruction study; instead, it focuses on prompting, AI understanding, and student attitudes.

The main conclusions are that the workshop was well received and associated with reduced perceived realistic and identity threat from AI, more positive than negative emotions after interaction, and student-reported improvement in the quality and clarity of ChatGPT interactions after learning prompting strategies. Students appreciated ChatGPT’s responsiveness and usefulness but also noticed important limitations, especially repetitiveness, lack of natural conversational quality, and difficulty following requests precisely. The authors conclude that hands-on AI literacy workshops can help students develop more critical and realistic views of LLMs, but they emphasize that the pilot nature of the study, technical issues, and limited sample require larger and more controlled future research.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a small pilot pre/post field study in one high school classroom (n=21) without a control group, randomization, or direct validated academic learning outcomes. It provides empirical evidence with clear methods, but credibility is limited to a single-group exploratory design.
impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest promising but unclear impact: there were statistically significant improvements in AI attitudes and perceived interaction quality, but no reported effect sizes and no direct K-12 literacy achievement outcomes. Overall impact is positive but modest/uncertain for the target literacy-use agenda.

interventions.use_case: High school AI literacy workshop using ChatGPT as a conversational 'personal teacher' on democracy content, with explicit instruction in prompting strategies so students can experience both improved prompting and the limitations of LLM outputs.

finding.finding_summary: Students used ChatGPT to learn and discuss concepts of democracy in a classroom task, and after prompting instruction they perceived the second interaction as better, clearer (mean=5.25, SD=1.11), and slightly more natural (mean=4.55, SD=1.61). However, the study did not report direct pre/post learning gains on democracy knowledge or standardized academic assessments, so evidence for academic improvement in this subject-area outcome remains indirect and perception-based.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of interaction quality during a democracy learning task; no direct content-learning assessment reported
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.11 to 1.61 for selected comparative perception items

finding.finding_summary: The two-hour workshop was associated with reduced negative attitudes and threat perceptions toward AI. Realistic threat decreased from pre to post (mPre=4.17, SD=1.39; mPost=3.73, SD=1.42; n=20; p<0.05), and identity threat also decreased (mPre=4.08, SD=1.39; mPost=3.57, SD=1.54; n=20; p<0.05); after interaction, students reported higher positive than negative emotions (mPositive=3.48, SD=1.79 vs. mNegative=1.35, SD=0.91; n=21; p<0.05).
finding.measure: Pre/post threat perception scales about AI; post-interaction self-reported emotions
finding.std_deviation: Realistic threat SD pre=1.39, post=1.42; identity threat SD pre=1.39, post=1.54; positive emotions SD=1.79; negative emotions SD=0.91

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved students' perceived ability to interact productively and critically with an LLM by teaching prompting strategies and highlighting AI limitations such as unreliability and constrained understanding. Students rated the second interaction as better (mean=2.45, SD=1.19 on the comparison item as reported by authors), clearer (mean=5.25, SD=1.11), and somewhat more natural (mean=4.55, SD=1.61), and qualitative evidence suggested a better grasp of limitations and more structured prompts over time, although no direct performance rubric for prompting skill was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived interaction improvement, perceived understanding of ChatGPT capabilities/limits, qualitative analysis of student reflections
finding.study_size: n=21; uploaded chat logs for 9 students
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.19 to 1.61 for selected prompting-related comparison items
